newsitem.title: FRANCE: France to develop Chirac's Mideast "breakthrough".
newsitem.headline: France to develop Chirac's Mideast "breakthrough".

text.p: France will take steps in the near future to develop President Jacques Chirac's bid to win a place for Europe in the Middle East peace process, Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on Sunday.

De Charette said Chirac, who returned home on Saturday, had already written to his European Union colleagues to brief them on his week-long tour of Syria, Israel, Palestinian territories, Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt.
Officials said Chirac, who is seeking a place for Europe as co-sponsor of the peace process alongside the United States, had also written to U.S. President Bill Clinton.

"We are going to take initiatives in the coming weeks and months, and these initiatives will have a single aim: help the peace process between Israelis and Palestinians so that this region reach security and development for all," de Charette told France 2 television.
He gave no details, but said he would urge his EU colleagues meeting in Luxembourg on Monday to appoint a special envoy to the Middle East.

He told the weekly Journal du Dimanche that the EU, as the main contributor of aid to Palestinians, must play a role in the peace process. "Europe cannot accept that it is to pay without taking part," he said.
He said Chirac had created a new momentum for peace and pulled off "a formidable breakthrough" whose historical dimension would become increasigly patent within weeks.

De Charette said there was a demand among Arab countries for a French presence in the peace process, and dismissed criticism in a television debate that Chirac was perceived in Israel as espousing radical Arab positions making him unlikely to mediate.
He said hardline Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu had been more open to a French role in private talks with Chirac than he apeared to be in public.
"France has chosen its camp: the camp of peace...France is attentive to both sides. France loves both sides," he said.
But he admitted France had work to do to persuade Israeli public opinion that it was not biased. "Our ambition is to be understood by the Israeli people. Some progress needs to be made," he added.
He insisted on France's friendship with the Jewish state, saying its main concern was for its security.

De Charette repeated France's position was based on implementing the Oslo and Taba Israeli-Palestinian accords, and on the principles of exchanging land for peace and allowing Palestinians self-determination.
